title: AI Feedback: A Thermometer or a Thermostat?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou questions the assumption that AI is an obvious fit for generating student feedback, arguing that before optimising AI-generated comments for accuracy, we first need to ask what feedback is actually for. Using Dylan Wiliam's thermometer/thermostat metaphor, she distinguishes feedback that merely measures a problem (a thermometer) from feedback that actually changes the underlying behaviour (a thermostat), and quotes Wiliam's example of a student told to 'be more systematic' who has no idea how to act on that accurate-but-useless advice. Her central worry is that current AI feedback development is pouring effort into making written comments more accurate, when the deeper problem -- prose comments rarely provoke real behavioural change -- remains untouched; she extends the critique to a broader pattern in AI evaluation research, arguing that studies showing AI helps professionals do existing tasks faster don't ask whether those tasks were valuable in the first place. She closes by previewing future posts exploring how No More Marking is developing new AI tools aimed at producing feedback that is both accurate and genuinely useful.
points: Christodoulou's thermometer/thermostat distinction (via Dylan Wiliam) gives a precise diagnostic for a problem every teacher senses -- accurate feedback that students can't actually act on -- and applies it directly to AI feedback tools.

Her core critique of the AI feedback research agenda -- that improving accuracy is like 'improving the precision of your thermometer' while expecting the heating to click on -- exposes a category error in how AI feedback quality is typically measured.

The Wiliam student anecdote ('I don't know. If I knew how to be more systematic, I would have been more systematic the first time') is a concrete, quotable illustration of accurate-but-useless feedback that any teacher will recognise.

Her extension of the critique to AI evaluation research generally -- that studies measure whether AI can replicate professional tasks faster, not whether those tasks were valuable -- broadens a feedback-specific argument into a more general methodological warning about AI research.
quotes: New artificially intelligent large language models like ChatGPT are really good at writing.
The classic metaphor here is of a thermometer and a thermostat. A thermometer measures the temperature. A thermostat uses the measurement to change the temperature.
I don’t know. If I knew how to be more systematic, I would have been more systematic the first time.
Written comments are not good at doing this. They are much more like a thermometer than a thermostat.

To extend the metaphor, using AI to improve written comments is like spending all your time improving the precision of your thermometer – and expecting that will magically lead to the heating clicking on or off.
We evaluate it by seeing if it can reproduce something that professionals currently spend a lot of time on. We don’t ask whether the thing the professionals are spending time on is actually valuable.
